newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran's Khatami seen facing conservative opposition.
newsitem.headline: Iran's Khatami seen facing conservative opposition.

text.p: Iran's president-elect Mohammad Khatami, seeking "powerful, innovative, fresh-minded" ministers for his cabinet, could face strong opposition from conservative clerics when he presents his government, political sources said on Monday.

Khatami, a 54-year-old moderate Shi'te Moslem clergymen elected by a landslide on May 23, is due to take over next month from President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, who must step down after the maximum two four-year terms allowed by law.

He has given no public hint as to his cabinet choices and in his first televised report to the nation said at the weekend he would choose people who were "powerful, innovative, fresh-minded and devoted to the country's development, justice and independence".

The former culture minister also called on all Iranians to respect the vote of the majority -- a non-too subtle jab at the conservatives who dominate most state institutions including parliament and whose hardline speaker he defeated in the election.

The 270-member national assembly holds power of veto over Khatami's cabinet selection and could block some of the more liberal-minded technocrats and centrists who were instrumental in securing his election, political sources said.

Iranian newspapers have said Khatami was being pressured by conservatives demanding they be consulted over the choice of ministers. Political sources said conservative clergymen and their allies had continuously warned against the new president's inclination to choose people from among his campaign supporters.
These comprised a rainbow coalition of centrists close to Rafsanjani and left-wing Islamists who rode a tide of popular desire for change after 18 years of Islamic revolution.
Khatami, due to be sworn in on August 3, has said he would look beyond factional barriers in picking his cabinet. His backers say he does not owe anything to any political faction.
Some reports have referred to a list of 2,000 figures being evaluated by the president-elect's office for potential roles.
Media speculation on Khatami's choices have focused on some high-profile figures already prominent in the Islamic republic.
- Mohsen Nourbakhsh, a former economy minister who is governor of the central bank, tipped to return to the economy ministry or become a senior aide to the president.
- Gholamhossein Karbaschi, mayor of Tehran, put forward as a possible interior minister.
- Mohsen Aminzadeh, Khatami's deputy when he was minister of culture and Islamic guidance during the 1980s, a possible candidate to replace Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati.
- Kamal Kharazi, Iran's ambassador to the United Nations, tipped by some others to be foreign minister.
- Mohammad Mousavi Khoeniha, a leading left-wing cleric tipped for the information (intelligence) ministry.
- Fatemeh Ramezanzadeh, a left-wing Islamist and one of the few women in parliament, tipped for the ministry of labour and social affairs.
- Behzad Nabavi, former minister of heavy industries and a founder member of a left-wing Islamist group, possibly Iran's next oil minister.
